P22: The Amish let their young people make the decision to join the church on their own when they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. While Rumspringa isn't as universal or as wild as pop culture makes it out to be, it's still a big deal that they're baptized as adults, because then belonging is a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.
P23: If the kids never leave, there's no way for the community to know whether they'd come back freely. Let them study, travel, make friends, see other ways of living, and disagree with the founders. None of that should get them treated like traitors.
P24: Every childhood narrows the future. Very few parents are going to hand their kid a bunch of money on their 18th birthday and say, "Here, go see the world." Most will help their kids get ready for some next step that can actually work. And a poor or money-free community may have even less to give, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
P25a: So the realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's just that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. If kids grow up without using money, they especially need to learn how the money world works, so they can function in it if they leave: jobs, rent, contracts, banks, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help.
P26: And some of them might split off, either permanently or into their own communities with different values, instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.
